newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - HUNGARY CENTRAL BANK RATE HIKE SHOCKS MARKET.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - HUNGARY CENTRAL BANK RATE HIKE SHOCKS MARKET.

text.p: The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) surprised the market with a deposit rate hike on Monday, but dealers and analysts said the move was to protect savings and did not signal an end to repo rate cuts.

The NBH on Monday raised the rate at which it accepts deposits from the commercial banks for six months to 21.00 percent from 20.75, breaking the trend of the central bank's almost regular monthly rate cuts in the past few months.

Interbank dealers said the NBH move shocked the markets on which repo cut expectations in the past two weeks substantially reduced liquidity and pushed up interbank rates, encouraging the banks to take advantage of current high NBH repo rates.
"(The hike) hit the market like a bomb," said Commerzbank dealer Sandor Tolonics.
He said the NBH move indicated its intention to keep forint savings more attractive than foreign currency savings which offer 19 percent yield for one year.
"If forint interest rates are too close to the yields from foreign currency savings, many investors may say that they prefer the greenback," Tolonics said.
NBH President Gyorgy Suranyi said on Friday that the NBH was determined to keep one-year Tresury bill yields close to the current levels of about 20 percent, to protect savings.

Postabank Securities analyst Attila Torok said the rate hike was a signal of the NBH's concern about real interest on mainly longer than one-year government papers as these rates seemed to be low compared with inflation expectations.
"They want to grab the interest on longer-term papers," he said. "The NBH would like to prevent a capital outflow and a larger spontaneous interest rate change (fall)."

He added that the central bank's introduction of the six-month deposit facility two months ago was already a signal of NBH resistance to quick interest rate change, but the market did not react and the the NBH had to move again.
Interest rates in Hungary have been dropping almost continuously since the beginnning of last year, in line with a 10 percent drop in year-on-year inflation.

Inflation is currently running at 18.8 percent and the NBH expects it to go down to 17 percent by December, while the government and the NBH said they would consider a further cut in the monthly devaluation rate from 1.1 percent in July.
Dealers and analysts said the NBH rate hike cooled expectations of repo cuts but did not end them.

"Now it is all uncertain," said Takarekbank money market dealer Istvan Zsolyom. "But the short term repo rate may be still cut a little. Other people may think that too as there was quite strong demand for one- and three-month money."

However, following the six-month deposit rate increase, the expected cuts in the NBH's one-week and one-month reverse repo rates may not come Monday afternoon, but rather in the next few weeks, dealers said.
The NBH changes its repo rates ussually on Monday at around 1300 GMT.
